question_text: In February 2018, KFC closed most of its UK restaurants after a change of delivery partner left it without the one item it is famous for. Police in two cities had to ask the public to stop phoning them about it. KFC turned the crisis on its head by taking out a two-page apology ad which featured a modified logo. So witty was this response that the campaign won a Gold Lion at Cannes and became a benchmark of crisis communication. What did KFC do?
answer_text: Switched KFC with FCK, on an empty bucket.

question_text: If you mix Jack Daniel's, Johnnie Walker and Jim Beam, you get a shot named after a famous Biblical story. What is the name of this drink?

AMOS (A Moment Of Sweet) is a novelty confectionery company behind Shakitz, gummies you shake in sour powder, and Peelerz, gummies you peel before eating. Another of its products, TastySounds, is designed to entertain more than one sense at once using the body's biomechanics. What exactly is TastySounds?
answer_text: A Music Lollipop (an AudioLollipop that lets you listen to music through your teeth via bone conduction)

question_text: In 1959, nine experienced hikers died on a Ural mountainside after fleeing their tent in the night, some without shoes, and with injuries that didn't match typical avalanche deaths. In 2021, two Swiss researchers simulated how a block of snow would hit sleeping bodies, and their results reproduced injuries like those found. For the snow, they adapted code written for another purpose, and for the bodies, they used car-maker crash tests on cadavers from the 1970s. What was the original, much more innocent creation for which this simulation program was developed?
answer_text: To animate realistic snow in Disney's Frozen (2013)

question_text: The land beneath X was first meant for a new opera house. In 1928, Columbia University leased it to John D. Rockefeller Jr. for the Metropolitan Opera, but the 1929 stock market crash made the Met pull out. He kept the lease and signed RCA as the anchor tenant instead, and X was first named after it. In the 2000s, Y made a show modelled after their former workplace, as an homage to X. Identify X and Y.
answer_text: X: 30 Rockefeller Plaza ("30 Rock"); Y: Tina Fey

question_text: A closed-end fund was named for Asia's fast-growing "_____" economies, and in one year three-quarters of its money sat in four of them: Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore. It traded on the NYSE under a three-letter ticker that works as a playful reference to its name. Give the ticker.
answer_text: GRR, the ticker for The Asia Tigers Fund

question_text: In 2017, the BBC profiled a group in Ghana whose members have a decidedly solemn job, but who nevertheless do it with a flourish. In early 2020, clips of someone in a precarious situation, followed by clips of this group and set to an EDM track called "Astronomia", started going viral. As lockdowns spread globally, the clips took on a second meaning, a warning to stay at home. While the whole world was collectively grieving, this group brought much-needed whimsy and smiles to people. What are we talking about?

Andre Geim is a Russian-born, Manchester-based physicist. He once used a powerful magnet to float a live frog in mid-air, exploiting the weak repulsion that the water in living tissue has for a magnetic field. The experiment became wildly popular, although as a curiosity more than as science. Around 2004, he and a colleague took a lump of graphite and peeled it repeatedly with ordinary adhesive tape until only a layer one atom thick remained, isolating a material now counted among the strongest ever found. That work got him the highest recognition of his field. What distinction does Andre Geim hold?
answer_text: The only person to have won both a Nobel Prize and an Ig Nobel Prize

question_text: In the 1999 remake of The Thomas Crown Affair, a bored billionaire steals Claude Monet's San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk from New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art, then has one of his own paintings, a Pissarro, hung in its place. A Surrealist painting hangs in his study and appears on a museum's exhibition poster. When the police close in, he fills the gallery with dozens of men in identical long suits and bowler hats while hiding their faces, so that none can be told apart from him, in a nod to that painting in his study. Name the artist who painted it.
answer_text: Rene Magritte (the painting is The Son of Man)

question_text: A songwriter woke from a dream with a complete melody and, worried he'd stolen it, spent months checking it wasn't someone else's. Until he found real words, he sang a placeholder lyric about a "Scrambled eggs", followed by "how I love your legs", so often on a film set that the director threatened to remove the piano. A bandmate helped him settle on the now famous one-word title. What is this song which also inspired an eponymous 2019 movie?
answer_text: Yesterday (by The Beatles; the melody came to Paul McCartney in a dream and he feared he had plagiarised it)

question_text: Human history is full of partnerships with animals, but nearly all of them involve domestication. Far rarer is a wild animal, with no training, choosing to work with people. First written about by a Portuguese missionary in 1588 and long dismissed as hearsay, one such partnership was confirmed in a 2016 study in Science. In Mozambique's Niassa reserve, Yao hunters make a trill followed by a grunt, a call passed down from their fathers. A bird, called "the greater X-guide", answers by flying from tree to tree ahead of them, guiding them across the bush, and the call more than triples their chances of success. Both sides come away with a share of the prize X. What is X?
answer_text: Honey (the bird is the Greater Honeyguide)

question_text: Thanks to the 1953 movie, in popular memory, X is a cheerful, mischievous hero of children's stories who guides the young ones who need it. But in the original 1911 novel, the author paints a darker side: the number of his followers varies "as they get killed and so on", and when one of them seems to be growing up, which is against the rules, the hero "thins them out". Despite the darker undertones, the author seems to have believed in the good in the world. Because when asked to help a London children's hospital, he gave it something nobody expected: all the rights to his most famous creation, on condition that the amount it earned never be made public. ID X or the creation.

Legendary architect Frank Lloyd Wright's largest public project is the Marin County Civic Center in San Rafael, California, a complex of county offices and courts. It has a sky-blue roof, a golden spire, and arches wide enough for cars to drive through. Everything about it is clean, ordered and precise, so far ahead of its time that it was chosen in the 1990s as a stand-in for a society run on order and perfection, which discards anyone it deems "not valid". Where have we seen this building? (The slide shows a photo of the building's distinctive long, arched, sky-lit atrium corridor with red balconies.)
answer_text: Gattaca (1997), as the headquarters of Gattaca Aerospace

question_text: Following is a list associated with a certain sporting record and the respective year when the record was made: 1950: 26 years; 1952: 23 years; 1955: 18 years; 1958: 15 years, 6 months; 1991: 15 years, 4 months; 1994: 14 years, 4 months; 1997: 14 years, 2 months; 1997: 14 years, 0 months; 1999: 13 years, 10 months; 2002: 12 years, 7 months; 2021: 12 years, 4 months. What is the sporting record being tracked here?
answer_text: Youngest person to hold the Grandmaster (chess) title. Currently the record is held by Abhimanyu Mishra, NJ, USA (12 years, 4 months, 25 days)

question_text: In 1966, two rival bodies agreed to merge, and a committee was asked to name the showpiece fixture that would pit their respective winners against each other. One of the participants, a team owner, blurted out a nickname without meaning it to stick, apparently because his children were obsessed with an ultra-bouncy rubber toy from the makers of the Hula Hoop and the Frisbee. The merged body's head disliked it and pushed for alternatives, but the media and fans embraced it, and it became official within three years. What is this name, now the title of an annual sporting fixture?
answer_text: The Super Bowl. The nickname came from the Super Ball (Wham-O), via Lamar Hunt.

question_text: About 4,300 years ago, an Akkadian king who ruled over Sumer boasted that ships from three distant lands tied up at the quay of his capital. Two lay along the Persian Gulf and are identified with Bahrain and the coast of Oman. The third, far to the east, supplied carnelian, lapis lazuli and rare timber. A cylinder seal in the Louvre belongs to an official described as an interpreter of that land's language, and carnelian beads etched with white patterns, thought to come from there, were buried in royal tombs at Ur. By what name did the Sumerians know this land, a name that gained fresh popularity in the 2010s through a work of fiction?
answer_text: Meluha (popularised by Amish Tripathi's novel The Immortals of Meluha)

question_text: Tie-breaker: On Friday, 2 January 2026, a Polymarket account that had joined only weeks earlier bet about $32,000 that one world leader would be out of office by 31 January. Prices on that outcome had sat low for weeks, as there did not seem to be an imminent threat to the leader's position. In the early hours of the next morning, a dramatic announcement by another world leader turned the odds on their head. The account walked away with more than $400,000. Who was the leader "removed" from office?
answer_text: Nicolas Maduro, President of Venezuela, captured by the US military
